title: A second round of the gambling duty rise
headline: Do the Budget 2025 online gambling rise again. If it raises the same: £1.1bn.
description: Budget 2025 raised Remote Gaming Duty from 21% to 40% and introduced a 25% Remote Betting Rate. Campaigners want more from online gambling. This does the same again: a further rise of the same size on the same duties, assumed to raise what the Treasury certified for the first round, year by year. Nobody has costed it.

baselinePolicy.text: Remote Gaming Duty 40% from April 2026; Remote Betting Rate 25% from April 2027; bingo duty abolished (Table 4.1 line 60). The package raises £1.1bn in 2029-30.

lines.title: Gambling Duty: Increase Remote Gaming Duty to 40% from 1 April 2026, introduce a new Remote Betting Rate at 25% (excluding Self-Service Betting Terminals, spread betting, pool betting & UK horseracing) from 1 April 2027, and abolish Bingo Duty from 1 April 2026

rawSource.note: Repeat: the Treasury's certified costing for the Budget 2025 package, taken as the yield of doing it again, year by year. Positive scorecard values reduce borrowing; here receipts positive means more revenue. Effects before the start year are not applied.

caveats: Nobody has costed a second round. The first took Remote Gaming Duty from 21% to 40%; a second of the same size would take it towards 60%, where operators' own margins and the black market start to matter far more, so the true yield would be lower and could be much lower.
The Treasury's costing is on the OBR November 2025 forecast, not the March 2026 baseline used here; the difference is small relative to the figures.

considerations.text: The Treasury's costing for the first round already allows for operators passing the duty on in worse odds and some players moving to unlicensed sites. A second round of the same size starts from a duty rate almost double the old one, so both responses would be larger. The figure here is the first round repeated, not a costing of the second.

The duty is paid by online operators on their gross profits and reaches players through worse odds and fewer offers; heavy online gamblers are more often men on lower incomes, which is the campaigners' case for the tax and the reason its yield is uncertain.

interactions.text: Reversing the first round and adding a second makes no sense together; the two cancel.
